items.question: How do you achieve pure abstraction in Java?
items.answer: Answer: Abstraction can be achieved in two ways: with abstract classes and with interfaces. Abstract classes have a limitation when you want pure abstraction (100% abstraction), so to achieve pure abstraction you use an interface.

items.question: What is an interface?
What problem occurs when different classes do the same work with different method names?
What is standardization, and how does an interface give it?
items.answer: Answer: Standardization means that all the classes use the same method signature. The interface declares one abstract method, and every class that implements it must follow that same signature, so developers have to remember only one name. Standardization comes automatically when you go for pure abstraction, just like gravy comes complimentary with a biryani in a restaurant.

items.question: Solve the Calculator1, Calculator2 and Calculator3 problem with an interface. What is the output?
Are interfaces abstract by default? Do you need to write the abstract keyword?
What is the default access modifier of a method inside an interface?
items.answer: Answer: If you write nothing, a normal class method would get package (default) access, but inside an interface Java adds public. So the method is public and abstract by default.

items.question: What happens if the implementing class does not use public while overriding an interface method?
Can you create an object of an interface? Can you create a reference?
items.answer: Answer: You cannot create an object of an interface, because it is abstract by default, and you cannot create an object of something abstract. But you can create a reference of the interface type. Calculator c = new Calculator(); // compilation error: object of interface Calculator c; // valid: only a reference Compilation error: error: Calculator is abstract; cannot be instantiated

items.question: What is the difference between tight coupling and loose coupling?
items.answer: Answer: In tight coupling the reference type is the child (implementing) class type, so the child object is referred to by its own class type. In loose coupling the reference type is the interface type and the object is the child class object. Loose coupling is polymorphism, and it is also known as upcasting. Calculator1 c1 = new Calculator1(); // tight coupling Calculator c2 = new Calculator1(); // loose coupling (upcasting)
